newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Water shortages plague Palestinians.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Water shortages plague Palestinians.

text.p: Their home sits above an underground lake of fresh water, but Mahmoud Abu Libdeh and his seven-member family are parched.
Abu Libdeh, 40, lives in Jenin, a city under Palestinian self-rule but still dependent on Israel for water supplies which municipal officials say barely drip through because of weak pumping power.
The Abu Libdeh family home has been without running water for more than two months. The children wear dirty clothes and the garden is dying.
"Would anyone believe that providing my children with water has become a problem? Water is God's gift but we cannot find it," Abu Libdeh said.
"We ration water, using it for absolute necessities. We have to count every drop when we wash our clothes or when we take a shower. We rarely water our garden," he said.
Jenin, whose Arabic name means city of gardens, sits on the northern West Bank aquifer stretching across the border inside Israel. But the city was hit by a serious water shortage last summer.
Mayor Walid Abu Mweis said the state-owned Israeli water company, Mekoroth, does not pump enough water to meet the needs of his city of 38,000.
Only a fraction of the 6,100 cubic metres (215,400 cubic feet) of water which are supposed to be pumped to Jenin every day actually reached the city because of low pumping power.
Abu Mweis charged that Israel had turned a deaf ear to his pleas for more water, fearing it would affect supplies to Jewish settlements.
Asked about the allegations, a Mekoroth official said the company would pump more water if a new well it drilled in cooperation with the European Union proved to be successful.
"We will start pumping tests to develop the well. I hope that this will be finished in one month to 45 days," said the official, Shmuel Kantor, who deals with water supplies to the West Bank.

Water shortages are common in the West Bank. But the problem appears to be especially acute in Jenin this year. Residents have been forced to buy water from contractors who fill tanks from springs with no health supervision.
The high demand has created a black market, prompting the Palestinian Authority to fix the price and deploy policemen to enforce it.

Hisham Istaitiyeh, deputy director of Jenin hospital, noted a sharp rise in stomach diseases due to contaminated water. He said water shortages had interrupted hospital work. Surgery cases are often postponed and patients go without a shower.
"How can a hospital operate without water?" he said.

Water shortages also affected agriculture, once the mainstay of one of the most fertile West Bank districts. Officials at the agriculture department estimated that vegetable production this year dropped by a third as a result.
Israeli officials attribute the problem to a general water shortage which they say affects both Palestinians and Israelis.
"The area in general is short on water. Aquifers are sinking and the quality of water is deteriorating," said Raanan Gissin, spokesman for the Israeli Ministry of National Infrastructure.
"But there is an agreement that allows Palestinians to drill for water in coordination with Israel," he said.
But Palestinians said the problem lay in unfair water distribution and pointed to lush lawns and shimmering swimming pools in Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza.
Palestinian researchers estimate that Israel pumps more than 85 percent of West Bank water across its border or to settlements.

Israel recognised Palestinian water rights under a 1995 self-rule accord, but retained full control of water resources. Water is a key issue in future Israeli-PLO talks on the final status of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
"The Israeli side must learn to share water with us just like they share the air," said Zuhdi Mansour, a Palestinian negotiator on water.
